Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

Vignette:
Manh Truong is a sixty-year-old Vietnamese American fisherman who has worked the Gulf Coast waters out of a small Louisiana port town for nearly three decades. He came to the clinic at the urging of his wife, who told the intake coordinator that her husband had not been the same man since the storm two years ago — that he slept in the chair by the window most nights and barely spoke at meals. Manh himself sat quietly through much of the first session, his hands folded in his lap, and when he finally did speak, he described what happened with the flat precision of someone who had rehearsed the facts many times in order to keep the feeling out of them.

The event occurred during a sudden squall that caught Manh and his younger brother, Tuan, offshore before either of them could make it back to the dock. The two men had fished together since childhood, first in Vietnam and then, after resettlement, along the same Louisiana bayou channels their community had made their own. When the water turned and the boat began to take on waves, Manh was at the stern securing equipment. He heard Tuan shout and turned in time to see him go over the side. Manh threw a line, reached over the rail, and for a moment felt the resistance of his brother's grip — and then nothing. Tuan was not recovered for two days. Manh was pulled from the water by a neighboring vessel, hypothermic but alive. He has never fully accepted that distinction.

In the weeks after Tuan's death, Manh returned to work because he did not know what else to do with himself, and because the bills did not pause for grief. But the water had become a different place. The sound of waves slapping against the hull — a sound he had heard ten thousand times and never once registered — now produced an immediate and overwhelming physical response: his chest would tighten, his hands would sweat against the wheel, and his body would flood with something that was not quite fear and not quite rage but contained elements of both. On rougher mornings, he would sometimes have to grip the rail and breathe until the sensation passed, aware that the other men on the dock could see him and not knowing what they made of it. The smell of salt air carried the same charge. Even the particular grey-green color of the Gulf on an overcast day was enough to bring it on.

At home, the nights became their own difficulty. Manh found that he could not sustain sleep — he would drift off and then surface again in the dark, heart already moving fast, sometimes certain that he had heard something, sometimes not knowing what had woken him. He began spending the early morning hours in the chair near the front window, watching the street, which felt safer than lying still in the bedroom. His wife would find him there at dawn and say nothing, because she had learned that speaking about it made him withdraw further.

What Manh found hardest to articulate, and what seemed to cost him the most to say aloud, was the feeling that had settled into him like sediment since the funeral. He had come to believe, with a quiet and immovable certainty, that he should not be the one who was alive. He and Tuan had been equally skilled on the water, equally experienced, and yet Manh had been at the stern and Tuan had been at the bow, and that was all the difference there was. The randomness of it offered him no comfort. If anything, it made the guilt heavier. He also described a growing sense that the people around him — neighbors, the men at the dock, even relatives — could not truly be trusted with what he carried, that they would say the right things and mean none of them. This had narrowed his world considerably. He had stopped attending the community gatherings at the Vietnamese Catholic church his family had belonged to for twenty years, and his wife had eventually stopped asking him to come.

What finally brought him in was a conversation with his adult daughter, who told him plainly that she was frightened for him. He sat with that for several weeks before calling. He said he did not expect to feel better. What he hoped, in the most guarded way, was to feel something again — because what frightened him most was not the grief itself, but the spreading numbness beneath it, the sense that whatever had been most alive in him had gone into the water with his brother.
